utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday, July 9th, 2008. Good morning to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to the witness. I hope you had a pleasant evening. And good morning as well to the OTP and to everyone assisting us in this case. Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, the Trial Chamber will read out a brief oral ruling. This is a decision for clarification by the Chamber with respect to timekeeping at the hearing. The Trial Chamber noted at the hearings of the 7th and 8th of July, 2008, that the Prlic Defence repeatedly stated that its questions were follow-up questions to those of the Judges. In order to avoid any misunderstanding as regards timekeeping at the hearing, the Trial Chamber wishes to stress the following: When a Defence team adopts a question asked by a Judge and asks, as they are called by the Prlic Defence, asks follow-up questions, time used to ask these questions will obviously be deducted from the time granted to the Defence team in question. In other words, when a Judge puts a question, the time used will be deducted from the Judges' time, of course, and not from the Defence time; but then if the Defence takes up that question again, that time will be deducted from the Defence time. I believe that this clarification was necessary. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just raise one preliminary thing before Mr. Karnavas begins, and that's to introduce the Trial Chamber and the other counsel to a couple of new faces that are here in the courtroom this morning. Anthony Hucklesby on my immediate right is an legal intern with the office of the Prosecutor; and on my far right is Ronnie Ervin, and he's working with us as in intern with our trial support unit. And these gentlemen have been assisting me in preparing the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you for introducing these two new members of your team, and welcome to them in this courtroom. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I begin, I do wish to note my objection to the Court's ruling. I don't think that it is in keeping with prior proceedings for the following reason: When, for instance, a Judge asks a question in my direct, it takes me in a different direction and I have to go back. It takes some time. And, so, while at the same time the Judges do have all the right to ask questions, if a Judge asks a question which puts the witness in a different direction and I have to get them back, now I'm being asked to use additional time, time that I had not planned, in keeping with formulating my direct examination. That being said, I understand your ruling. I've continuously said in the past, Your Honours, that none of us would want to be tried this way. None of you would want to be tried this way, but that's neither here nor there. Having said that, originally we had planned eight hours for this gentleman. It is obvious to us that we cannot complete our task in six hours. You gave us a certain amount of hours. We did not challenge that decision, recognising that it is a discretionary matter on your part to decide how many hours the Defence would put on. And barring, you know, something extraordinary, we recognise that the President of the Tribunal is not going to overturn a discretionary issue such as time allotment, in keeping with his obligations to the United Nations and the Security Council as a result of the completion strategy. Having said that, at this point in time, I wish to ask that we be granted an additional hour for this particular direct examination. Obviously, we're not asking an additional hour to the hours that have been allocated to us. It would be within the hours that you gave us. And to compensate for that, we do anticipate dropping one or two witnesses or proposing that they come in as 92 bis. So we believe we will be able to complete our task. We also have in mind of reserving several hours for just in case what other witnesses are being brought for other teams, in order to elicit positive information versus, you know, confronting them. So, at this point, we wish to ask for an additional hour, again to be taken from our overall hours which were granted to us. We believe that these are our hours, and it's up to us to determine how to utilise them, recognising that at the end, we have to live with the consequences of the decisions that we are making right now. And, again, I didn't mean to be disrespectful by saying that, you know, there are times when you take the witness in a different direction, but that's my opinion. And, in any event, I was told that on follow-up questions, time was not being taken out. That was what my original understanding was. Anyway, that's my request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. With respect to the additional hour, of course, it will be granted to you because that's part of the overall time that was granted to you by the Trial Chamber; and you know that the Appeals Chamber confirmed the decisions taken by the Trial Chamber in that respect. So you're perfectly entitled to use an additional hour; but, of course, we are in charge of keeping time in this case, and this time will be deducted from the time you would have had for other witnesses. It's your choice. If you need an additional hour, you will be granted that additional hour. We have nothing to say about the matter. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps I failed to say good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, so good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As you heard, we are under certain time restraints, so I will beg you, beg you, to at times give me shorter answers; and when necessary, I will ask you for complete answers. If we could continue, I believe we were on the topic of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly, if you go to 1D 0201, 1D 0201 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that this is a decree on the application of the law on regular courts. It's dated 23 December 1992? And, again, this would be consistent with what you told us previously yesterday; that is, for all intents and purposes, there were no substantive changes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was that 1D 0201 or 1D 02001 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There were two 00s, sorry. 1D 00201. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, is it the Law on Regular Courts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have that under 2001 in the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But if you look at the top of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 2001, I have a decision to appoint the Croatian Defence Council-- oh, no. That's 2061.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it may be that there may is a mistake on the -- there may be a mistake in the label, but it's 1D 00201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, sir, could you, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In this specific case, this is a decree on the application of the Law on Regular Courts. It has to be emphasised that the HDZ-HB did not abolish any regular court, nor did he establish any new regular courts. This decree served to take over the organisation of regular courts that was prescribed by the Laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the only exception being the Department of the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And if we look at Article 10, it shows that the operation of the court is being financed out of the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because there was no other possibility of financing in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that this is December 23. It's a decision on the allocation of funds for the need of the Department of Justice; and, here, we see that on behalf of the HVO, Dr. Jadranko Prlic has signed this decision. You would confirm this, would you not, that this is -- this decision was passed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is a HVO decision on the allocation of the funds for the judiciary. I believe that this referred to the -- or was used for the redecoration of the Court in Mostar to which the Municipal Court of Mostar was moved, after the JNA attack on Mostar, during which the building of the Municipal Court of Mostar had burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decision to appoint -- on the appointment of the assistant of the head of the Judicial, Justice, and General Administration; and we can see the gentleman who was being appointed. Can you confirm that the gentleman was appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on the appointment of my assistant for criminal and disciplinary punishments, and he was an attorney from Mostar, Aid Glavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us again, for the record, whether he was a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's dated 15 January 1993, 15 January 1993. This is -- as we can see, it's pursuant to Article 5 of the decree of the establishment of a branch of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of Herceg-Bosna. And if we look at Article 1, we can see there's a decision here taken by the HVO that was signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and we see the appointments of certain individuals. Can you confirm that and can you please tell us, of the individuals that were appointed to this branch of the Supreme Court, how many of them are Croats and how many are Muslim, or Serb, or other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is a decision and the appointment into the Department of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, headquartered in Mostar, which is a relocated Department of the Republican Court. And we spoke at great length about this court yesterday. People who were appointed, and there were seven of them, seven judges, four of them were Croats and three were Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. I read eight names on this list, and I would like the witness to identify the names he says are names of Muslim judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Indeed, there are eight names on the list, and the following are Muslims, Bosniaks: Semir Pusic from Mostar, the president of the court; Alija Zaklan, a judge; and Mehmed Sator, another judge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, normally speaking, a Supreme Court has several chambers or sections, depending on the countries. You may have a constitutional chamber, an administrative chamber, and so on and so forth. But here we are talking about a branch of the Supreme Court. What does that mean? Is that branch specified in a specific area of the law, or is it just a branch dealing with everything which is a sort of a subsidiary of the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina that is located in a different area from Sarajevo? Because here I read that the so-called "branch" is to be established in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a general department with general jurisdiction, rather than a specialised chamber; and we spoke about that yesterday. I don't know whether my answer today satisfies you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to your knowledge, this Supreme Court, and I note with great interest that the president of the Court is a Muslim, but this Supreme Court, did it have to rule on any kind of proceedings? Did it deal with any proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The department passed all the decisions, depending on the case. As you may well know, in certain cases, this department issued decisions in a chamber composed of three judges, which was the most common case. The laws often prescribe that decisions were adopted by three judges in a chamber, but there were also situations in which there was an independent judge passing decisions or five judges in a chamber. All situations were possible, but the president, as an individual judge, could only pass decisions which concerned the internal affairs of the court itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand your testimony from yesterday, then today, this branch of the Supreme Court essentially functioned as the third instance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that it was necessary, under your legal system, in order for certain cases to be finalised, they had to go through the third-instance court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to save some time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in common law, you're right; but we are sitting here in an international court, and the Judges are qualified enough to decide how far the question can go. And here the question is so obvious that even if it's a leading question, we may allow it. So, please, Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I start my answer, please? We've already said that this was a third-instance court. However, there were cases in which the higher court in Mostar issued the decision in the first instance; and then the Supreme Court appeared as an appeals court, but it could also appear as a court issuing extraordinary legal remedies. So two options were possible. It could act as a second-instance court or a third-instance court, sitting on certain extraordinary cases which called for the protection of the legality, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, again, just to make sure it wasn't lost yesterday or the day before when I asked you the question: Decisions that came out of this branch of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they ever -- to your knowledge, were any of those decisions overturned after the formation of the Federation as a result of the Washington Agreement or, later on, after the Dayton Peace Accord?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No decision of the Supreme Court was ever overturned for the reason of the lack of competence of this department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly the question that ought to have been asked prior to the last question. Was there any remedy against a judgement of this Bench of the Supreme Court to a higher instance, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An appeal could be lodged to the Constitutional Court, or the Chamber for Human Rights was allowed, but this never happened. No decision was ever the subject of any appeal procedure, let alone being overturned by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this may be of some assistance to Judge Trechsel as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accord, were there internationals involved in overseeing the judiciary, especially -- was there an Ombudsman office as well, to deal with any such matters where there might have been complaints, perceived complaints of violations of human rights or any other rights?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the Washington and Dayton Accords, both the Ombudsman office and the Court of Human Rights were established, and there were eight foreign judges participating in those. Some of them were even members of the Human Rights Court in Strasbourg. The composition of this court that acted as the Chamber for Human Rights was eight foreigners, seven locals. The president of that court was Michel Picard, a foreign national.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go on to 1D 02379, 2379.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here is a decision dated 15 January 1993, and it's for the selection of certain judges to the Lower Court in Stolac. Can you confirm that the HVO took this decision that was signed by the then-president, Dr. Jadranko Prlic? And can you please tell us whether any of the judges that were selected for that court were Muslim; and if so, who and in what position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on the first selection of judges for the Lower Court in Stolac, as may be seen in the document. Three judges were appointed, of whom one was Bosniak, Muslim; and two Croats. The Bosniak member was Edin Beca, the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to 1D 01898.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is 16 January 1993; and, here, we see that it's for -- the following judges were elected to the Bosanski Brod District Military Court. If we look to the second page, we see that it is signed by the then-head of the Defence Department, Bruno Stojic. And can you confirm that this decision -- this proposal, I should say, not decision, but can you confirm this proposal? And in looking at some of the names, can you confirm that there are Muslims who are being proposed to sit on these courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is not a decision; this is a proposal by the Defence Department, i.e., the head of the Defendant Department, for the appointment of judges for the District Military Court in Bosanski Brod. This is a proposal for the appointment of five judges of whom -- actually, six judges, of whom five are Croats and one is a Muslim, Bosniak. He is under number 4, Fuad Perlice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then we see there is another list of elected judge jurors, and then -- and for some of us, we may not be familiar with that concept. What is it a judge juror? Is that a layperson who serves, also, along with professional judges?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A judge juror is something that could be similar to the persons who serve in the Anglo-Saxon system. They are laymen. They don't have to have legal education. But there were situations in which there was a judge sitting independently with two lay jurors. So they are actually lay jurors. They're not legally educated persons. And there were also instances in which there was a chamber of three judges which could also have an additional two lay persons sitting as judge jurors. In practice, they were just making up the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next number, 1D 02382, 2382.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, here, we see that this is a list of employees of the Mostar Lower Court who are under work obligation during January 1993. And we know that there was a general mobilisation, so that individuals 18 to 60 had to respond. Can you please tell us what "work obligation" means for those who may not be familiar with the concept?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best. The system of All People's Defence then, in the former Yugoslavia, implied that in peacetime every person of age had their war assignment. As soon as a person became of age, that person was given a war assignment. That war assignment could be one of several things: One could be an assignment to a military unit, another to a unit of Territorial Defence, the third one could be into a unit of civilian protection, or the fourth option was the so-called work obligation. In such a system, "work obligation" meant that people who were under work obligation during a state of war were not duty-bound to serve in any of the military units or any of the units of the civilian protection or Territorial Defence. That duty to serve was discharged in their company or an institution they had worked for up to then. In this particular case, these are the judges for whom eight was envisaged that their obligation would be work obligation in court. In other words, they would continue to discharge their judicial duties. Thus, the HZ-HB, for all the judges who were judges before the war, regardless of their assignment, even if they had been assigned to a military unit, the HZ-HB introduced work obligations for them, which means that even if one of the judges had been mobilised, we, as the department, asked for these persons to be demobilised and returned to the court in order to continue performing their judicial duties. And as may be seen from the list, all the judges of the Municipal Court in Mostar performed their judicial duties. And even if some of them had been assigned into the army, we asked for them to be demobilised and returned to their original duties. My answer may have been too long, but I don't know how else I could have explained this term "work obligation," and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You spoke of judges, but also here we see "Administrative Technical Section," and we see court registry officers, typists, cleaners. Were they -- based on the answer that you gave us, were they also employed by the courts and simply continued working under this work obligation, or are these new people that are being brought in to fill those positions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the cases, those are people who performed the same duties in the court even before the war. I would like to say that of the 12 judges who were on the list as the judges of the Basic Court in Mostar, eight were Muslims, Bosniaks; three were Croats; one was a Serb; and the president of the Basic Court in Mostar was also a Bosniak, a Muslim, Ziba Nozic. The HZ-HB never changed this composition. And now, with regard to a question I was asked yesterday, before the war, this Basic Court in Mostar had 23 judges, of whom 11 Serbs, eight Muslims, and only four Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understand correctly, this Lower Court that existed, prior to events prior to the war, continued after January 1993, but what seems to me important, and you pointed this out because it was not obvious for the Judges, is that this Lower Court will function after January 1993 with a majority of Muslim judges, including the president, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. The Basic Court or the Municipal Court of Mostar continued working in the same composition, save for the fact that some of the Serbs had left, together with the JNA. I suppose that we will see that later. Based on the structure of the Higher Court in Mostar, we will see what happened to them. All the other judges who had been appointed to the Municipal Court in Mostar remained in their positions, and this is the composition that the HZ-HB accepted. Just a while ago, when we spoke about the decree on regular courts, we also said that the HZ-HB did not establish any new regular court, nor did it abolish any regular court. But I need to emphasise here that since the building of the Basic Court in Mostar had burnt down, they were moved after the month of January, and we saw that funds had been approved for that, to the building of the former building of the Court of Associated Labour that had been reappointed for that purpose. And all that was done because the former building of that court was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that this Associated Labour building that housed the tribunal destroyed by the Serbs was in Mostar West or East?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the border between East and West Mostar, but it was in East Mostar. It was destroyed at the beginning of the war in May 1992. I believe that it was destroyed by the shelling on the part of the JNA, Then it caught fire and burned to the ground; and all the documentation of the court was also destroyed, as I told you on the first day of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. During the conflict in Mostar, we know there was a frontline, the HVO on one side -- can you hear? I repeat. During the conflict, there was a demarcation line or a frontline. How did the defendants go to the court? Could Muslims travel to see the judges? And vice versa, could the Croats go to the court to meet the judges, to meet their lawyers? And you, as a lawyer, during the conflict did judicial activity continue? Were there trials, hearings, proceedings, and rulings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a time of fierce fighting in Mostar, during which nobody could go to any courts, either Croats or Bosniaks, because both buildings in the vicinity of this separation line were inaccessible. Therefore, during the peak of the conflict, neither Croats nor Bosniaks could access any of the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to follow up, Witness, here, just to follow up, it sounds now as if the courts were not working, practically, during the conflict period or during a certain period. Could you give us more information on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said this, I meant the period between May 1993 and sometime up to mid-1994. During that period of time, if these courts were operational at all, it was just the judge on duty who went there, and they could, indeed, do very little. They could not perform their duties properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would this also apply to Western Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This applies to Croat judges and Bosniak judges, and to citizens of both Croat and Bosniak origin. Because of the location of these courts, of their buildings, on the very separation line, the access to neither of the courts was possible. What we tried to maintain was to provide access to the buildings for the judge on duty and the prosecutor on duty for the most urgent cases. It was possible, from the Bosniak side, to hit every person in any of the court buildings from infantry weapons, and the same was possible from the Croat side. What I'm saying is that this could be done from both sides. Anybody in the court buildings could be a target. And the buildings themselves were very damaged, and it had very few window panes. Both court buildings had very few window panes left. I'm basically speaking about the Basic Court, the Higher Court, as well as the Municipal Court and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Municipal Prosecutor's Office and the District Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about 1992, were the courts working then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1992 until mid-1993, that is, until the outbreak of the fiercest fighting in Mostar, both the Municipal Court in Mostar and the Higher Court in Mostar, and both prosecutors' offices, continued to discharge their functions. And as you can see from this list, they were able to do so with the number of staff listed here. So the Municipal Court in Mostar did not work with full capacity because we said before the war there were 25 judges; but in this -- in this period, there were 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at this document, and if you look at the second page -- well, if you look at the original page, this is a list of judicial employees who received salaries for the month of 1993 -- January 1993, and we've already seen some of the names. Could you please tell us what positions these individuals held - and we do see a disparity in the payment - just very quickly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you hear me? In this specific case, we have judges and prosecutors who were assigned to the Municipal Court and the Municipal Prosecutor's Office in Stolac. The difference in salaries results from the fact that Edin Beca was the president of the Court, while Niko Moro was the Municipal Prosecutor. The person under number 4 was his assistant, and numbers 2 and 3 were judges. So the difference in salaries is accounted for by their respective positions. The president of the Court had a higher salary than a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at now the next document, 1D 02383, 2383, this is 4 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You'll see at the very top it's the Department of Justice and General Administration. At the end of this document, we see the name of the president of the Court, Mladen Barbaric. And I just want to focus everyone's attention, and particularly your attention, to paragraph number 3 on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, have you been able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously, Mr. Buntic has not heard me, and that time should not be used against me. It must have been at least five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Buntic, now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going back to this document, 1D 02383, and let us focus our attention now on paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says: "According to the guidelines from the Ministry of Justice and the General Administration of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a wartime staffing plan was prepared in June 1992, with a total of 41 employees (one court president, 14 judges, and 26 staff)." Now, could you explain to us a little bit about this particular paragraph in 1D 02383, because it says clearly that at least there are some guidelines that are being applied from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, we are dealing with information that, at my request, was provided by the president of the Higher Court in Mostar. And he informs me that according to the wartime staffing plan, a wartime staffing was established according to which the Higher Court in Mostar must have a president and 14 judges; while in peacetime, the prescribed number was 19 judges plus the president, so 20 in total. He also provides information about the identity of the 14 judges who, according to the wartime staffing plan, were to continue working as judges. He provides a list of the judges, from which it is obvious that in the composition of the then-Higher Court in Mostar, there were six Muslims, Bosniaks; five Croats; two Serbs; and one Jew. Can I please continue about the composition before the war? Before the war, there were eight Muslims, six Serbs, five Croats, and one Jew. I'm saying this to supplement what I said yesterday; namely, that regardless of the population make-up in Herzegovina, that is the jurisdiction of this court in Mostar where Croats were in the majority, Croats were represented only with 20 per cent in the composition of the judiciary. I'm not sure if I need to provide the names because I know the ethnicity of each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not necessary, unless the Judges want. We do need to move a little bit quicker, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. There seems to be a very important item, which is the conclusion of the letter of Mr. Barbaric, because he refers to Judge Nada Dalipagic; and he states that this court, from the presidents of the Republic of Bosnia, received no document nor the Official Gazette, for that matter. So we have the impression that this judge, who is the president of the Court, states very clearly that they are cut off from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Sarajevo, and we can draw the conclusion that he's trying to make due as best he can. Do you think that this last sentence correctly summarises the situation in which these judges found themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true, Your Honour. The president of the Higher Court in Mostar confirms in this sentence all that we have discussed earlier, that is, yesterday; namely, that there was absolutely no possibility for the Official Gazette to come from Sarajevo to Mostar. I'm talking about official channels. Whether it could be smuggled somehow across the separation lines, I don't know about that; but mail could not reach Mostar from Sarajevo, including the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it there are no questions from the Bench concerning the use of the guidelines from the Ministry of Justice in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That being so, I'll move on to the next document. 1D 02381.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very quickly, we see a list of employees, Lower Court, who are under work obligation? You already explained to us what the "work obligation" meant? Can you confirm, given your position, that this is accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Here, again, we have a list of judges and staff of the Municipal Court in Mostar, submitted by the president of the Basic Court, Mrs. Ziba Nozic; and it is the list is provided for the purpose of payment of salaries to the judges and staff whom the president of the court had found to have worked in that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the judges, and then we can look at the typists and what have you, If you could tell us how many of the judges, for instance, are on this list are Muslim; and then do the same thing for the typists and anyone else that you see on the list.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we said a moment ago, this list included -- includes seven Muslim judges, four Croat judges, and one Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The president of the court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the court continued to be Mrs. Ziba Nozic. She had been appointed to this position before the war, and she was never relieved by any enactment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or any other body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the land registry officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are talking about the same person. Maybe you meant the registry books that we managed to save from the fire in the Municipal Court in Mostar. They were relocated during the war to Citluk and returned after war to the Municipal Court in Mostar. Is that what you meant, the registry books, land registry books?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. We're on this document, and we're looking at the names, Mr. Buntic. Very quickly, if you look at number 13, and then if you look at number 23, you know, we're trying to get an assessment because the allegations are that this whole region was Croat-ised and ethnic cleansing is going on. So this is the purpose of all of this. It may not make sense in a normal setting to be discussing it because that's crude fashions, but we must do it in this case.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. Under number 13 and number 23, we see Amira Nozic and Mustafa Velagic. They are land registry officers; that is, persons who were in charge of and were authorised to enter -- to make entries into the land registry books, recording ownership of real estate. They continued in their positions during the war. Nobody replaced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is very important, because if you try to Croat-ise an area, you're obviously going to ethnically cleanse even in those departments. So what is their ethnicity, sir? That is the point I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the statement or argument of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's based on the Prosecution theory which we've heard for two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. It' an argument. It's actually a tirade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, help us out here, because the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO of which you were the minister of justice, is being accused of having ethnically cleansing even in the court system. Could you lease tell us here how many of these positions are Muslim? That's why I asked concretely the land registry, which is a rather important position.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I didn't understand the question at first. Both are ethnic Muslims, Bosniaks. On the staff of the Court, there are seven Muslim judges, four Croats, and one Serb; whereas, in these other services, both the land registry officers are Bosniaks; whereas, among other staff, I could go through them one by one, but I believe it's obvious, from the list itself, that there are Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. All three ethnicities are represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00274.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is just as an aside for the Judges to get a better understanding. Here, we have the president of the municipal HVO in Livno appointing a Dinko Galic, who is an engineer, to be the acting president of the Livno Municipal Court. And, perhaps, you could explain to us how is it that an engineer is being appointed to be none other than the president of a misdemeanor court in Livno?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this may cause a laugh in the courtroom, but you have to understand that there were no other solutions in that situation. As you saw yesterday, we had to organise a district military court, a district prosecutors' office in Livno, to preserve the operation of the Municipal Court. Until that time, the position of the misdemeanor judge - I believe his name was Mr. Bravo - who is appointed to the District Court, we had to assign him to the Municipal Court, a regular court, after which this position of the misdemeanor judge was vacant. And there was no one with a law degree in Livno or in other places to fill this vacancy. A similar situation was in Tomislavgrad, where throughout the war the court had to function only with one judge, that is, the president, Andrija Kolak. There were no other people available, so the only option was to appoint an engineer by training until a list became available with someone from a law degree to fill this vacancy. Maybe I'm too lengthy, but it's not easy to answer with a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you here. Could you just explain to us, very briefly, in one sentence - you don't have to go on for 20 lines, just one sentence - how is it that it is the president of the Municipal Court of the municipality of the municipal HVO that is making the appointment for this municipal misdemeanor court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Council was in charge of that before the war and during the war. The Municipal Council was always the one who appointed misdemeanor judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to have to cut you off on occasion, Mr. Buntic, if you're going on, because we just need concrete answers. I want to speak about January 15, 1993, in particular, this decision that was rendered by the HVO, and I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it very much, if the Defence has completed the topic of the judiciary, I would appreciate it very much if the Court would allow me to make a brief statement regarding this topic, the operation of the judiciary, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to confer with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Karnavas, after considering the matter, the Trial Chamber believes that if the witness wishes to supplement answers given to your questions, then that time should be deducted from your time. So it's up to you to decide whether you want your witness to give additional information on that particular topic, or you may think that what has been said so far is sufficient for the Judges and you decide to move on to another topic. It's up to you. I know that I'm putting you in quite a tricky position, but you've seen worse than this and you'll see worse than this in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that I will ask one general question, and that might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, is there anything else you wish to tell us about the judiciary before I move on to the next topic? Make it brief, if possible.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two minutes. Your Honours, over the past three days, I gave evidence about a great number of regulations, decisions, and documents in the spirit of the judicial system; and I, therefore, ask to be allowed to make this brief statement about the way in which the judiciary of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna operated in reality. For that purpose: I, Zoran Buntic, before this Court and under oath, hereby state: If this Court, in the course of these proceedings, finds that any judge appointed by any body or agency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and regardless of who proposed the appointment, had committed any act punishable under the Statute of this Court, I, Zoran Buntic, former representative of the General Administration Department in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, assume hereby the responsibility for any such acts and hereby invite the international prosecutor here present to issue an indictment against me. This statement also applies to any action taken by my deputies and my assistants. This statement does not apply to the judges appointed by the Wartime Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so help me God. After this, I would like to briefly explain this statement that I've just made. In the work of the courts and judicial departments of the General Administration, there was absolutely no interference whatsoever by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or any of the accused here. On the contrary, within the limits of what was possible at the time and their own capacity, they contributed to the functioning of the judicial system. I led my department independently on my own to the best of my abilities and with good intentions. My deputy and my assistants discharged the functions assigned to them with due diligence and performed my instructions. So within -- with my full mental capacity and without incitement from anyone, I decided to make the statement that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic. I'm sure we all appreciate those remarks and observations. We now want to switch to January 15, 1993, and I'll refer to document P 01155, P 01155.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We've seen this document before in this court. This is dated January 15, 1993. It's a decision taken by the HVO, signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic. And is it safe to say that you are familiar with this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. And as far as I know, a day or two after this decision, the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina made an order that was very similar to this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you -- were you in Mostar on 15 January 1992 when this decision was issued?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 15th of January, 1993, I was not in Mostar. At that time, I was coming back from Geneva, where I had attended negotiations concerning the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. I heard of this decision on TV. I believe that on the 15th, I was somewhere in Zagreb or on my way home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to walk you through step by step. So if you could please tell us, what exactly did you do in Geneva, who were you with, and what, if anything, was reached, decided?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Geneva, I know that I was there with Mr. Akmadzic, and I believe there was somebody from the military. Akmadzic and I dealt with civilian issues, civil affairs. I believe there was also someone from the military staff of the HVO, where they talked about military issues with the Bosniak delegation; whereas, our team discussed the future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina. We had reached an agreement on the text, and I remember that this text was, indeed, a great insight with the constitutional principles along the lines of the Vance-Owen Plan. I believe it was harmonised, as well as the military agreement. I believe the military agreement was also reached, but I'm not sure about that. I believe, in fact, our agreement was certainly agreed and initialled in Geneva. I believe the same is true of the military agreement, but don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 00818.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is dated 18 January 1993. And if we look at the names, we do not see you there having been a participant. We see others, but we don't see you. And, of course, if we just look through this, these minutes, we see that at some point there is a discussion concerning communications that were had between Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Dr. Jadranko Prlic. My first question is: Were you present on the 18th of January, 1993, when there was a discussion, there was a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you can see from the record, my deputy, Karlo Sesar, attended. I returned a day or two later. On the 19th or perhaps 20th, I was back in Mostar, but not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the next document, which is P01227, these are the minutes on the 19th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, here, we do see your name. Can you confirm to us that you did, in fact, attend the extraordinary session that was held on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I attended this session, as you can see from the minutes. I returned on the 19th. I wasn't sure a moment ago whether I returned on the 19th or the 20th; but from the minutes, you can see I was there on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you have been briefed, incidentally, by your associate, your deputy, about what, if anything, had transpired the previous day during that extraordinary session on 18 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me briefly what had been discussed at that session. He told me there had been a session a day earlier and what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Have you had a chance to look at this particular document, the one of 19 January 1993; that is, P 01227? And can you confirm to us whether the minutes, as stated, truncated as they are, whether they reflect what was being discussed at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the minutes are done properly and reflect what had been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we look at 1D 00820, this is dated 20 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a letter from Mr. Mate Boban, wherein he indicates that he wishes to -- for certain changes to be made to the decision that had been issued on 15 January 1993. Were you aware of this, sir, at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw this document for the first time when you showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were changes -- were changes made to the decision of 15 January 1993 subsequent to your arrival in Mostar? And we saw that you were there on the 19th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you were able to see, I was in Mostar already on the 19th. This document is of the 21st, and I was back in Mostar already on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going back to the decision of January 15, what was your understanding of this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you already that I had been in Geneva for negotiations about the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, that certain matters were resolved there, agreement was reached about the basic constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that the military agreement was also reached. I don't know the details of that agreement. But what Mr. Akmadzic and I were told was that everything had to be done to put an end to the war between Bosniaks and Croats, and that that was not possible without separating the warring sides. I was told that that agreement contained provisions about the separation of the two sides, and I saw this decision in that context. It's not an order to anyone. It requires a certain conduct on both sides, and that in areas which have a majority population, one of the armies had to be withdrawn, units of the HVO had to withdraw from provinces 1, 5, and 9. So it's not prejudicial to any of the sides, because provinces 3, 8, and 9, and 10 were considered to be majority Croatian, because indeed they were. It was not possible to leave both armies in one area. One had to withdraw. Provinces 1, 5, and 9 were majority Bosniaks, so it was clear that Croatian units had to be subordinated, as it says here, to the VH Army, in order to have peace, to restore peace. The presence of both armies in one locality, in one region, is impossible. I'm saying it's impossible, because it will always lead to a conflict. There is no civilian authority that is able to control them and maintain peace if they continue to be in the same area. That's my opinion, my position, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go on to our next topic, this deals with districts. We'll try -- I don't know if we can deal with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if I look at the time, it might be more prudent to have a break at this point, before I start the next chapter, because it's impossible to do it in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. It's 25 past 10.00. The best is for us to have a break now to allow Mr. Karnavas to prepare for the next topic, and we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the Prosecution wishes to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We just wanted to take a brief opportunity to raise a couple of timing-related issues with the Trial Chamber in respect of this witness, because it's clear that we're going not only deeply into this week but perhaps deeply into next week with Mr. Buntic. I don't know, at this point, what other examinations the other Defence teams have planned. We have some information from the Coric team which I'd also like to raise. But with respect to the following witness -- actually, the following two witnesses, and I don't know whether they are both open session or not, and whether I don't know if I can say the names - I know Mr. Zuzul is - but we don't know how we're going to accommodate the witnesses who are scheduled for next week, given the way it's going with Mr. Buntic. And if, in fact, there's going to be any adjustments made, it would be very helpful to the Prosecution to know. That's my first point. And if I could just raise the other, then the Trial Chamber could hear from the Defence. We've been -- yesterday, we were given notice by the Coric team of its intention to use some exhibits with this witness, Mr. Buntic; and it appears to us to be a situation which the Prosecution's being placed in the position of having to perhaps cross-examine him or follow up with Mr. Buntic on areas that are outside the scope of his direct examination or which otherwise are certainly matters which we should have been given more notice about. These are registers, photos copies of registries from Mostar and Western Herzegovina. We can't read them, we don't have translations of them, I don't know how the Coric team intends to proceed in of this witness on direct. But the indications from the Prosecution perspective are that this is going to lead to something that we haven't had sufficient notice about or sufficient ability to prepare for in cross-examination, and it's possible we're going to be asking that this witness be brought back to The Hague at a later time, after we've had sufficient opportunity to prepare. I don't know, because I don't know what the witness is going to say and I don't know what the Coric team is intending to do. But it appears to us, based on the late notice of -- and the information that we have at hand, is that there's a good possibility that we're going to feel prejudiced by what's going to be happening during the so-called cross-examination of Mr. Buntic by the Coric team. And I just raise that now, and I asked the witness not be brought in because I thought it appropriate not to have him here while we talk about what the Coric team may or may not be planning to do with him on cross. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Madam, you may answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respond. These are from various prosecution offices from Herzegovina. Yesterday, we provided CDs of these documents, and we sent an e-mail showing what parts of these registers, and they are only several examples for illustration, and where they can be found. These CDs are on our 65 ter list. They have their number. On the 31st of March, they were submitted in a timely fashion. I believe that this witness spoke about the establishment of military prosecutors' offices, military courts, and also of the civilian judicial system. I don't want to overstep the boundaries of the examination-in-chief of this witness. I wish to show him the registries solely for purposes of identification. I want the witness simply to tell me whether these are, in fact, the registries, whether this is what the registers looked like; and there is no translation needed for that because this has been provided to the OTP. The list of abbreviations, we will ask him to explain. For example, His Honour Judge Trechsel yesterday asked what "KT" stands for; and for all the Judges, we have prepared a list. This is not to be tendered into evidence, but is simply an explanation of what is meant by "KT," or by "KF," and so on and so forth. We've also prepared the articles of the law mentioned in these registers, and I only want to show some examples. For example, where we have a criminal report or something else from a file, how this can be identified with a file number in the registry. I don't think this falls outside the scope of the examination-in-chief or that it requires preparation longer than one day. Yesterday, everyone, including Mrs. Majkovski and the Prosecutor and the Registrar received the list of every image from the register that we will refer to. And this can be then zoomed in, too, electronically, and one can see whether the numbers correspond to the numbers from the criminal report and the names of the persons concerned. That's all I wanted to say. That is what I will deal with in my cross-examination. There will be no surprises; and precisely for this reason, yesterday we provided this, and it's all on the list of the 31st of March. There's not a single document that is not on that list. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. As I 0understand it, these lists were forwarded on CD-ROM the 31st of March to the Prosecutor's Office. So the Prosecutor's Office is in possession of these registers since the 31st of March, so you've had them for several months, not since yesterday. Secondly, and personally, and I'm not committing my fellow Judges, but it's part of an investigation at the very least regarding justice, because it is stated in the indictment. The question of justice, we had to get the Prosecutor's Office to verify the list of prosecutors were on the ground. It wasn't done by the Prosecution but by the Defence, and now the Prosecution says it doesn't have enough time to prepare itself. So, since March 31st, you're in possession of these registers; but from what I understand, the legal counsel, she just wants a few minutes to determine that the prosecutors in question recorded the cases under the numbers "KT," "KF," et cetera, and the witness will say, "Yes, which proves that justice continued to operate." That's all she wishes to establish, and there's no need for weeks or even months to be able to cross-examine the witness on this. So on the first point, Mr. Karnavas, what is your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I was going to address this issue at the end of the -- at the end of the day today. I was going to ask for a couple of minutes just to brief this issue. We acknowledge that we are going to go into next week with this particular witness, and the following witness is an important witness. He is due to arrive shortly. He will be on standby until he goes on. I understand that we have Mr. Zuzul, who is expected to testify, who also come back, and it has been prearranged. And so we - Ms. Tomanovic and I - had concluded that it would be best to ask or to inform the Court that in our opinion, it might be best to postpone Mr. Zuzul's arrival until the following week, in other words, to start on Monday, as opposed to him coming on a Friday. This way, we have the following witness testifying, and then we don't start -- disrupt that in order to hear Mr. Zuzul and then go back. This way, we would finish the second one. Mr. Zuzul will then pick up from there, so he can be here to be ready for Monday. In other words, he would arrive here on Sunday, to be ready to testify on Monday. Monday is a full day, as I understand, the following Monday. And we still have another short witness after that. So based on our calculations, we're not going to be losing any time. As you can see, we're very, very efficient and very well prepared, even for these eventualities, and we welcome this intervention. However, I must say that in the future, we could save a lot of courtroom time if we just communicate to each other, especially with the second issue. There was no need to spend ten minutes. I think if they had a five-minute conversation outside the record, this matter could have been clarified; and then if they still needed to go on record to raise their objections of how they're being, you know, prejudiced, they could do so. But I think this could have been handled quite nicely. And right now, we've had all these people sitting around, international taxpayers' dollars being abused, in my opinion, on matters that could be handled with a tete-a-tete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this witness, we will end on Thursday with him. He will remain, and we will resume with him on Monday afternoon, July 14th; and then we will move on to the witness of next week, and we'll also have a hearing on Friday. So we should end with your witness on Friday, and then we will hear Mr. Zuzul on Monday morning and afternoon. Let me clarify because the Chamber saw the problem. We will end at 12.30 on Monday, so that people can have lunch, and then we will resume at 2.15 p.m., working until 6.00 p.m. in order to complete this. That's the timeline. As Mr. Karnavas indicates, the Prosecution and the Defence can settle that amongst themselves, and that will save time so we're not running behind. Everything is proceeding at a speedy pace. We can bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so the Trial Chamber's aware, by our records. The Prosecution has five hours for the cross-examination of Mr. Zuzul. The Prosecution intends to use all of that time, and so we still think that there's a likelihood that we will not be able to finish both of the witnesses during that final week before the summer recess. But, obviously, we'll see how things go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, normally, Mr. Stringer, with five hours on Monday, Mr. Zuzul, if there's no objections or numerous additional questions, we should end on Monday with Mr. Zuzul.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That would be our hope, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's no need for anticipatory anxiety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We must always be optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Or as the Jewish mother says, "I see it, I believe it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing resumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, again, good morning. We're going to move to the next topic dealing with districts; and, again, I'm going to beg you, I'm going to beg you to please, at times, be a little shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to look at 1D 00509, 1D 00509.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decree with the power of law on the power of work -- and work of districts. It's dated 13 August 1992 in Sarajevo. And just very briefly, are you familiar with this particular decree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the degree and I have -- I have an echo in my headphones. I have already provided my testimony about this subject by pointing out that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because of the blockade of Sarajevo and the central state bodies, and I'm talking about the Parliament, Presidency, and government, they were forced to pass a decree on the establishment of new bodies that would be functioning during the war. And it is of no essence what their names would be: The districts, as they're referred to by the Presidency, or the unions of municipalities, as we call them. As a lawyer, by trade, I believe that I'm allowed to note that the then-prevailing Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allowed for the association of several municipalities into unions, with a purpose of defending their territory; whereas, that same Constitution did not give the authority to the president to change the internal territorial organisation of the then-existing Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would kindly ask the usher to help me with the headphones. I'm am hearing an echo in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please stop the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was on the phone. I was wondering or I was hoping that he didn't -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, so, if I understand you correctly, what you're saying to the Trial Chamber here is that this decree, in your opinion, as a trained lawyer, familiar with the system in your country, and especially the Constitution, the then-existing Constitution, that this decree was unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. In my view and according to the then-prevailing Constitution, the literal territorial organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina could only have been changed pursuant to a decision by the Assembly, because this is a constitutional matter and the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not transfer that authority on to the Presidency. And if I may be allowed, I would like to read parts of Article 4 of this decree, if that would not constitute too long an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Before it is necessary to give us some further for information, I would like to ask the following: A decree has been adopted by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to know -- it was, of course, dated 13th August 1992. Now, the question is that if Mr. Buntic might be able to tell us: What was the voting, if any, voting results of the voting in the Presidency in view of the fact that there should have been also the then-Croatian members of the Presidency participating in the decision-making? So my question is if you know anything about the internal proceedings, what happened within the Presidency when the decree was adopted, and if the Croat members also voted for it. It would be important, in my view, because you said that it was against the Constitution; and then we have to look at it, how the Presidency adopted this decree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not familiar with these details. I'm not familiar with the way the Presidency passed this decree and whether at that session all the members of the Presidency were present. I just said that the Presidency did not have such constitutional powers because the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not transfer such powers on to the Presidency, according to the Constitution. This the exclusive power of the Assembly and could not be transferred on to the Presidency in war or in the immediate threat of war. Legal authorities could be transferred, but the matters that were regulated by the Constitution could not be transferred. The municipalities, themselves, could, however, issue a decision on association. They could associate themselves into a union of municipalities. For the Presidency to issue a decision changing the territorial organisation of the state, it was not possible, because it is a constitutional matter rather than a law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, but I simply would like to state that it would have been better then to attach that part of the Constitution which is relevant, as far as this very decree, and in order to show to us, to the Bench, that it was anyway against the Constitution itself. And, again, I say that since it was wartime and in wartime many of the provisions of the Constitution had been referred to the Presidency to act upon, therefore we should know, really, that according to the Constitution, according to the Presidency, according to the members of the Presidency, if this act of adopting the decree was legal or illegal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler, for that, and just let me respond very briefly to your observation. We try not to try the entire case through any particular witness. So we do -- and given the time constraints, we can't do that. I agree, in a perfect world, that's what I would do. But I have both my hands tied behind my back and one of my legs has been taken, and you're asking me to sprint. It's rather difficult. So we're put in a position where we have to discriminate. That's number 1. Number 2, we do intend to tie it up through another witness. However, that being said, we do welcome the judicial hint. We welcome that there's an issue that you obviously wish to hear from, and we will try to provide that information to you through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you wanted to make reference to certain portions of Article 4, so if you could do so rather quickly, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 4 says: "Within the areas that are regulated by republican regulations, the district or bodies within the purview of their duties and authorities may, if the interests of defence and protection and the agency of regulation of certain matters and relationships so require, issue regulations to regulate that matters and relationships of an immediate importance for the district should these regulations not be passed in due course by the Republican organs." And this quote points to the fact that the districts could also pass regulations from the areas that were within the purview of the Parliament of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we have the same case in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next document, and I believe the Trial Chamber has seen the next document, which is 1D 02565.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, here, we see that this is a letter from the Minister of Energetics, Mining, and Industry, and it's to a Mr. Demirovic. And in the first -- the first letter, we see that he's being asked to provide certain materials to Mr. Prlic. So Demirovic is the go-between to Mr. Prlic. If we go to the next page, we see that this is another letter. This one is from the vice-president of the government of RBiH, Mr. Ljubuntija. This is to the commander of the 4th Corps of the Army of BiH, in other words, the Muslim army; and, there, he's being asked to urgently implement the matter. This is -- we can see Dr. Jadranko Prlic is being copied. And then if we flip the page, we see this is on February 25th, yet you see another document. This time it's from the Ministry of Defence, the deputy minister, Mr. Bisic; and he is writing about the setting up of the Mostar-Livno district. This is February 25th, 1993. Now, let me stop right there. By February 25th, 1993, had the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna been set up and had it been operational for some time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at that time had already been established. It was operational, and I believe that it is interesting to point out that everything was happening at a time after the Vance-Owen Plan was signed in Geneva and accepted by both sides. That plan employed a completely different territorial organisation than the one that is being proposed and requested; i.e., whose implementation, even through military force and through a military commander, is requested by Vlatko Lugunja, vice president of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Hercegovina. I'm familiar with these documents. They were discussed at the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A little bit step by step, I want to slow down because it's rather interesting. The first decree is August 13; and now, several months later, it appears that the army now wants to implement this, the Ministry of Defence. And, of course, it's March 3, 1993, that Mr. Prlic is going to be noticed of this, at least that's what it appears from the first page of the document. And can you please tell us, from August 13 to March 1993 - it's August 1992 to March 1993 - can you please tell us whether any ongoing negotiations had been taking place concerning the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to which the representatives of the Muslim nation were discussing with the representatives of the Serb and the Croat nation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally participated in these talks and negotiations, which were conducted in Neum between the 19th and 23rd December, 1992. On the Muslim/Bosniak side, Professor Kasim Trnka was the head of the Bosniak delegation. Attorney-at-all Camil Salahovic and Mensud Borogovac from Tuzla were members of the delegation. I was the head of our delegation; and with me, there were also Professor Ante Margetic and Anto Valenta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Throughout this period, because it would appear that this is the first notice, did any representatives from Sarajevo come to share their views on how to implement this particular decree, especially if you look back to the decree at 1D 00509, if you look back to it, and you look at Article 5, which says: "Funds for work of district bodies shall be ensured in the Republic's budget."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I say this for the Trial Chamber's convenience because we heard from the Minister of Finance, and what we had learned was that there was no budget, to speak of, as a result of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So did anybody come from Sarajevo to explain how these districts were to work, how to implement this decree, and where the money would come from to pay the salaries for the judges, for the court system? So all the things that this piece of paper, this decree, claims are the responsibilities of these newly-created territorial districts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not privy to any document of that kind. Nobody ever spoke to me about the financing of these districts. So when I say "no document," I mean documents of a financial nature or talks about the financing of these districts. As for the rest of the issues, I was fully familiar with the issues when it came to these districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday, I believe we saw an interview - I can dig it up here - where you indicated that Alija Izetbegovic had been in Mostar, and that there was a 50/50 arrangement. You recall that interview, And we do know that Alija Izetbegovic was in Mostar in October 1992. Now, did Mr. Izetbegovic and his entourage, his colleagues, his collaborators, did they come with expert services to describe how these districts were to function, how they were to be organised, how to implement this legal instrument, and, of course, where they would find the money, the budget, in order to make these districts, these newly-created districts, function?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that nobody ever spoke to me about financing or wrote to me about financing. We never discussed the matter of financing, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not so worried about the wondering. I'm worrying -- I'm wondering whether they had somebody draft this decree. It's rather detailed. Obviously, when you draft such a decree, you have in mind how it's going to be implemented; otherwise, it's just empty words on a piece of paper. My question, again, concretely: Was there a delegation that ever came from the government of Sarajevo, the Presidency? Did they ever send a delegation to explain how to organise these districts, so at least you would have some sort of knowledge of how they intended to implement this particular decree which for several months went unnoticed until March 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that when it came to the implementation of financing and the implementation of this particular decree on the establishment of the districts, nobody ever spoke to me. I'm not familiar with any talks about that. I'm not familiar with the arrival of any delegation that was supposed to implement this. I'm familiar with these letters, and I know the documents arrived and were discussed. But as for some delegations arriving to implement things or to talk about things, I wouldn't know anything about that.
